title: NI's 64-week outpatient wait — the worst in the UK by far
narrative_md:
**If you live in Northern Ireland and your GP refers you to a consultant today, the median wait is longer than a year and three months.**

542,451 patients were on a Northern Ireland outpatient waiting list in September 2025 — more than one in four of the population. The median wait to see a consultant was 64.1 weeks. Equivalent England wait is 14 weeks. No other NHS system in Europe comes close.

The Northern Ireland health system runs on the same founding principles as NHS England but diverged structurally from 1973 with the creation of integrated Health and Social Care. HSC combines hospital, community and social care functions in five regional trusts, coordinated by the Strategic Planning and Performance Group (formerly the Health and Social Care Board, abolished 2022). In theory, the integrated model should deliver better outcomes than England's more fragmented structure.

In practice, NI's health performance has been the UK's worst on elective care for over a decade. The Bengoa review of 2016 diagnosed the problem: too many small acute sites, insufficient specialisation, and a workforce under-planned against demographic demand. Bengoa recommended consolidation of services into fewer, larger centres. The reforms were endorsed by then-Health Minister Michelle O'Neill and scheduled for 2017-22 implementation.

Then politics froze. The Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in January 2017 over the Renewable Heat Incentive scandal and was not restored until January 2020. It collapsed again in February 2022 over the Northern Ireland Protocol and was not restored until February 2024. Seven of the nine years after Bengoa were lost to Executive absence. Permanent secretaries held the brief without political cover to close a hospital or consolidate a specialty.

The NI Audit Office's June 2023 report described elective waits as 'at crisis point' and concluded the system had 'no credible plan' to recover performance within a parliamentary term. Waiting list volumes grew 33% between March 2020 and September 2025 — far outpacing English recovery.

Mike Nesbitt, UUP Health Minister since May 2024 in the restored Executive, published the Elective Care Framework in 2024-25 committing to a Bengoa-aligned regional consolidation. Its key moves: designating specific sites as Day Procedure Centres, protecting elective capacity from emergency pressure, and scaling cross-border commissioning with the Republic of Ireland under the Planned Healthcare Scheme (the post-Brexit equivalent of the EU Cross-Border Directive). In 2024, 3,700 NI patients received treatment in RoI private hospitals at HSC expense.

The fiscal context is narrow. The NI health budget for 2024-25 is £8.0 billion — 49% of total NI Executive Departmental Expenditure Limits. Any uplift competes directly with education, infrastructure, and justice. The November 2024 Budget settled NI with an additional £1.5 billion on needs-based adjustment from HM Treasury, but officials estimate that clearing the existing waiting list to English levels would cost £400-600 million annually for five years — a sum the Executive cannot find without cuts elsewhere.

The deeper obstacle is political. Every hospital consolidation under Bengoa would close or downgrade a service in a specific constituency. In a 90-member Assembly elected by STV in 18 constituencies, no Minister survives closing a local ward. The NI health crisis is, at root, a collective-action failure dressed as a management problem.

For 542,451 patients, it is also an ongoing medical emergency — one that the UK's worst waiting times statistics are unlikely to cure before the end of the decade.
